'''''Asplenium monanthes''''', the '''single-sorus spleenwort''', is a [[fern]] native to parts of Africa, islands in the Atlantic, the Americas and Hawaii. It belongs to the [[family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Aspleniaceae]].<ref name=kew />

==Description==

Here are key features of ''Asplenium monanthes'':<ref name=kew>{{cite web
| url = http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=200004143
| title = ''Asplenium monanthes'' Linnaeus. In Flora of North America North of Mexico (FNA)
| last = Wagner Jr.
| first = H.
| last2 = Moran
| first2 = Robbin C.
| last3 = Werth
| first3 = Charles R.
| volume = 2
| location = St. Louis, MO & Harvard University Herbaria, Cambridge, MA, USA
| publisher = New York and Oxford: Oxford University Press via eFloras.org
| access-date = August 31, 2026
}}</ref><ref name="af">{{cite web
| url = https://www.fernsofafrica.com/blank-species.php?species_id=102620
| title = ''Asplenium monanthes'' L.
| website = Pteridophytes of Africa
| last = Ballings
| first = Petra
| access-date = August 31, 2026
}}</ref>

*The erect-standing leaves' [[rachis]]es are reddish dark-brown/blackish throughout, shiny and hairless.
*The once [[Pinnation|pinnately]]-divided leaves usually are up to {{cvt|60|cm}} long, but mostly about half that, and up to around {{cvt|3|cm|frac=2}} wide. The leaves' 10-45 pairs of subdivisions, or [[Glossary of botanical terms#pinna|pinnae]], are strongly asymmetric, somewhat [[trapezoidal]], the leaf's middle ones up to {{cvt|17|mm|frac=8}} long and {{cvt|8|mm|frac=16}} wide, though typically smaller, with bases rounded to diminishing gradually to the attachment point. Pinna margins facing the leaf tip are toothed, while margins on the pinnae's lower side are toothless.
*A single [[sorus]] (rarely up to 3) occurs on each fertile pinna, always near the lower, toothless margin. Sori are slender to oval in outline, with a narrow, silvery scale or film of tissue, the "indusium," running along the pinna's lower margin. When the [[spore]]-producing [[sporangia]] are mature, they may hide the indusium.

At some locations the above details still may not be enough to distinguish ''Asplenium monanthes'' from similar species in the area. An obscure feature possibly helping to confirm the identity is that sometimes along the length of the rachis, two very narrow, silvery, filmy "wings" can be observed, especially with magnification; these are barely visible in images on this page.<ref>{{cite web
| title = ''Asplenium monanthes'' L.
| url = https://www.worldfloraonline.org/taxon/wfo-0001108056
| website = The World flora Online (2026)
| location = published on the Internet from various floras
| language = English and Spanish {descriptions}
| access-date = August 31, 2026}}</ref> Also, these filmy wings' margins do not bear tiny, pimple-like bumps, but rather are entire or slightly notched.<ref name="baj">{{cite journal
| last = Madrigal González
| first = Daniel

| first2 = Brenda Yudith
| title = Familia Aspleniaceae

==Distribution==
''Asplenium monanthes'' displays a scattered distribtion. In the United States, it occurs in the southern states of Arizona, North and South Carolina, Alabama and Florida, plus Hawaii. In the Caribbean, it inhabits the islands of Jamaica and [[Hispaniola]]. In Mexico it occurs nearly throughout, though not in the [[Yucatan Peninsula]]. In [[Central America]], it is found in Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Panama. In South America, it inhabits Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Brazil, Uruguay and Argentina. In Africa, it is found in Cameroon, Rwanda, Sudan, Ethiopia, Somalia, Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Malawi, Zimbabwe, South Africa, Lesotho and Madagascar. The spleenwort also appears in the [[Azores]], [[Madeira]], [[Canary Islands]], [[Bioko]], [[Gough Island]] and [[Tristan da Cunha]].<ref>{{cite web
| url = https://www.worldplants.de/world-plants-complete-list/complete-plant-list/?name=Asplenium-monanthes#plantUid-14427

}}</ref>

==Habitat==
In central Mexico at elevations of {{cvt|1400|-|2300|m}} ''Asplenium monanthes'' inhabits forests with [[pine]] and [[oak]], [[cloud forest]]s, and [[Secondary forest|secondary]] vegetation derived from those forests.<ref name =baj /> In Africa it is found on shaded floors in evergreen forests, often near streams, bamboo or [[podocarpus]] forest, and less often in forests along rivers or in [[heath]] zones near streams.<ref name=af /> In North Carolina, it is described as a species of [[grotto]]s and waterfalls requiring shade, high humidity or moist rock faces, and a cool [[microclimate]]. Though elsewhere usually it appears on [[limestone]], here mainly it occurs in cracks and crevices of [[Granitoid|grantic rock]].<ref>{{cite web
| url = https://auth1.dpr.ncparks.gov/flora/plant_list.php

==Uses by humans==

===In traditional medicine===
In Mexico's [[Sonora]] state women of the [[Guarijio people]] take a "tea" of ''Asplenium monanthes'' to stop menstruation and as a contraceptive.<ref>{{cite web
| url = http://www.medicinatradicionalmexicana.unam.mx/fmim/termino.php?l=4&p=guarijia&cr=6&t=flor-piedra&id=178

}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==

In 1767, [[Carl Linnaeus]] described and named ''Asplenium monanthes'' using the name it still has, noting that his [[type specimen]] originated from Africa's [[Cape of Good Hope]] (written as "''Cap. b. spei''", shorthand for "''Caput Bonae Spei''").<ref>{{cite book
| last = Linnaeus
| first = Carl
| title = Mantissa plantarum
| language = Latin 
| date = 1767
| pages = 130
| access-date = August 31, 2026
| url = https://bibdigital.rjb.csic.es/viewer/10315/?offset=#page=10&viewer=picture&o=bookmark&n=0&q=}}</ref>

===Varieties===

In 2026 these two varieties were accepted:<ref name =kew />

*''Asplenium monanthes'' var ''monanthes''
*''Asplenium monanthes'' var ''wagneri'' (Kuhn) Stolze

===The ''Asplenium monanthes'' fern complex===

''Asplenium monanthes'' is part of an "''Asplenium monanthes'' complex" comprising 22 species occurring mainly in [[Mesoamerica]], with its [[Vavilov center|center of diversity]] in southern Mexico. The complex is part of the "black-stemmed" spleenwort group, which also includes the ''[[Asplenium normale]]'' and ''[[Asplenum trichomanes]]'' Complexes.<ref name="a">{{cite journal

===Genetics and evolution===

''Asplenium monanthes'' is [[Apomixis#Apogamy and apospory in non-flowering plants|apomictic]]. This apogamy apparently has evolved independently multiple times, and has facilitated [[reticulate evolution]]. Moreover, the species is [[Polyploidy#Types|triploid]] and possibly sometimes tetraploid.<ref name=a />

===Etymology===

The genus name ''Asplenium'' is based on the Greek ''splen'', meaning "[[spleen]],"  because [[Dioscorides]] thought that a fern or ferns in the genus was useful for treating diseases of the spleen.<ref>{{cite web
| url = http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=102877
| title = ''Asplenium'' Linnaeus Boeckeler. In Flora of North America North of Mexico (FNA)
| last = Wagner Jr.
| first = H.
| last2 = Moran
| first2 = Robbin C.
| last3 = Werth
| first3 = Charles R.
| volume = 2
| location = St. Louis, MO & Harvard University Herbaria, Cambridge, MA, USA
| publisher = New York and Oxford: Oxford University Press via eFloras.org
| access-date = August 31, 2026
}}</ref> In the common name "spleenwort," the ''-wort'' is from Old English ''wyrt'', meaning "plant, root,"<ref>{{cite web
| url = https://www.dictionary.com/browse/wort
| title = wort
| website = dictionary.com
| publisher = Dictionary Media Group, Inc
| access-date = September 1, 2026
}}</ref>  thus "a plant for the spleen."

The species name ''monanthes'' is based on the Greek ''monos'', meaning "single, alone"<ref>{{cite web
| url = https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/mon-
| title = mon
| website = merriam-webster.com
| publisher = Merriam-Webster, Incorporated
| access-date = September 1, 2026
}}</ref> and the Greek ''anthos'', meaning "flower".<ref>{{cite web
| url = https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/anthes
| title = -anthes noun combining form
| website = merriam-webster.com
| publisher = Merriam-Webster, Incorporated
| access-date = September 1, 2026
}}</ref> In this case, an extended meaning of "flower" is conjured, that of "reproductive structure"—the fern's sorus. Thus, "a single sorus," aptly describing the single-sorus spleenwort.
